To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the r-process-enhanced stars are not all binary, and that (b) the binary fraction of the r-process-enhancement stars is indistinguishable from the binary fraction of Population I giants, and is therefore likely to be ~40%.

the radial velocities of a small subset of metal-poor stars with r-process element abundancerelatively to those of the elements of the iron-peak and below, are found to be periodic, and that these stars are therefore binary.

the r-process elements of metal-poor stars are not enhanced in binaries, and that the r-process enrichment was not a local phenomenon, but was im- printed on the natal clouds of stars that are single and in binaries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical tagging of r-process-enhanced stars in the primitive halo of the Milky Way.
understanding the chemical composition of stars in the Galactic halo and its relation to the early evolution of the Milky Way.
the chemical evolution and the binary properties of metal-poor stars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the r-process element enhancement of the stars in this sample is not the product of a binary companion, and thus the r-process enhancement of these stars is the product of an external source.

the binary frequency of r-process-enhanced stars is similar to the binary frequency of stars with similar metallicities, and that these stars have a similar binary frequency to that of stars in the Galactic halo.
the r-process element abundant stars are single stars and they have been enriched from the r-process in the ISM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found that the binary frequency for the r-process-element-enhance metal-poor stars are indistinguishable (within a factor of ~2) from those of Population II stars in general, and that the r-process element enhancement of these stars is not due to a binary companion.

the binary frequency of r-process-enhanced stars is indistinguishable from the binary frequency of Population I stars, and that the chemical signature of the r-process in the Galactic halo is not a local phenomenon.
the r-process element abundant ratios of these stars do not appear to be a result of a binary companion that has passed through the AGB stage of evolution or a supernova event.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the primitive halo of the Milky Way, r-process-element enhancement was a rare, but not unique, event in the formation of individual stars.
the r-process element abundaces of these stars were set at birth, and that the stars were not affected by mass transfer or supernovae in a binary system.
r-process-element-enhance metal-poor stars are not all binaries, and thus that the r-process enrichment history of the early Galaxy is more complex than previously believed.
